question_text: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She had a blood pressure recording of 148/94 mm Hg on her previous visit one week ago. Her home blood pressure log shows readings of 151/97 and 146/92 mm Hg in the past week. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. Her pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 150/96 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. The extremities are well perfused with strong peripheral pulses. Serum concentrations of electrolytes, creatinine, lipids, TSH, and fasting glucose are within the reference range. A urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question
                    A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She had a blood pressure recording of 148/94 mm Hg on her previous visit one week ago. Her home blood pressure log shows readings of 151/97 and 146/92 mm Hg in the past week. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. The extremities are well perfused with strong peripheral pulses. Serum concentrations of electrolytes, creatinine, lipids, TSH, and fasting glucose are within the reference range. A urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with persistent hypertension (150/96 mm Hg) and normal laboratory results, indicating no signs of end-organ damage or secondary causes at this stage. Given the absence of significant findings on physical examination and normal renal function, the most appropriate next step is to evaluate for secondary causes of hypertension. Plasma renin activity is particularly useful in assessing for renovascular hypertension, which is a common secondary cause. While an electrocardiogram can assess for cardiac changes, it is less relevant without symptoms or signs of cardiac issues. Polysomnography is indicated if sleep apnea is suspected, but there are no indications of this in the current case. Echocardiography and renal ultrasonography may be considered later if further evaluation is needed. Therefore, the best next step in management is to measure plasma renin activity to rule out secondary hypertension.
